Primary and secondary locations

Source: vignettes/locations.Rmd
locations.Rmd

A store can be kept in several places at once: for example in a cloud bucket that a team shares and in a local folder on each laptop, for fast reads and for work without a network. This vignette explains how rcs keeps these copies in step, and what happens when one of them cannot be reached or falls behind. It assumes you have read vignette("rcs").

library(rcs)

Primary and secondaries

Each place that holds a copy of the store is a location: a local folder, or a Google Cloud Storage address of the form gs://bucket/prefix. A connection has:

  • exactly one primary location. Its catalog is the truth: a dataset’s current version is the version the primary’s catalog names. Writes go there first.
  • any number of secondary locations. Each holds a full or partial copy. A secondary copy of a dataset is up to date when its version equals the primary’s.

The connection is not saved anywhere. Each script, or each user’s environment, says which locations it uses, so one person can read a shared bucket through a local copy while another works on the bucket alone.

Here three local folders play the three locations. In practice the primary would often be a bucket.

root <- file.path(tempdir(), "locations")
primary <- file.path(root, "primary")
copy_1 <- file.path(root, "copy-1")
copy_2 <- file.path(root, "copy-2")

st <- store_connect(primary, secondary = c(copy_1, copy_2), create = TRUE)
st
#> ── rcs store ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Locations:
#>   primary      local  <tempdir>/locations/primary
#>   secondary 1  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#>   secondary 2  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> History: off (store default)
#> Datasets: none

Writes land everywhere

store_write() writes to the primary and then to every secondary, in the order given. There is no argument to choose locations: a write always tries them all. Each location gets only the files it lacks, each file is checked by its MD5 checksum after the copy, and each location’s catalog is switched last.

store_write(st, rcs_sim_table(200, seed = 1), "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  key = c("shop_id", "date", "product"),
  partition = "year"
)
#> ℹ Writing "sales/daily": 200 rows in 2 files (partition year).
#> ✔ primary    <tempdir>/locations/primary  2/2 files sent  27.9 kB  0.2s
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1   2/2 files sent  27.9 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   2/2 files sent  27.9 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 2 files in 3 locations. Catalogs updated.

In the printed connection, the columns 1 and 2 show the state of each secondary copy: = the same as the primary, ≠ another version, – missing, ? location unavailable.

st
#> ── rcs store ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Locations:
#>   primary      local  <tempdir>/locations/primary
#>   secondary 1  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#>   secondary 2  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> History: off (store default)
#> Datasets: 1
#>   name     kind   rows     size  files  updated           1  2
#>   sales/
#>     daily  table   200  27.9 kB      2  2026-11-27 18:58  =  =
#> Secondary copies: = same, ≠ differs, – missing, ? unavailable.

Reads use the closest copy

A read picks, among the locations that hold the dataset at the primary’s version, a local folder first, then the primary, then the other secondaries. With a bucket as primary and a local folder as secondary, reads come from the local folder as long as it is up to date, and a line says so:

st <- store_connect("gs://my-bucket/store", secondary = "~/data/my-store")
x <- store_read(st, "sales/daily")
#> ℹ Reading "sales/daily" from secondary ~/data/my-store.

options(rcs.quiet = TRUE) silences that line. A secondary that is behind is skipped, and the read goes to the primary.

Addresses from the environment

Scripts often should not name the locations: they differ between users and machines. When primary is not given, store_connect() reads it from the environment variable STORE_PRIMARY, and the secondaries from STORE_SECONDARY, several separated by ;. A line like this in a user’s .Renviron file sets them for every session:

STORE_PRIMARY=gs://my-bucket/store
STORE_SECONDARY=~/data/my-store

The script then only says:

st <- store_connect()

Here the variables are set for one call:

st_env <- withr::with_envvar(
  c(STORE_PRIMARY = primary, STORE_SECONDARY = paste(copy_1, copy_2, sep = ";")),
  store_connect()
)
st_env
#> ── rcs store ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Locations:
#>   primary      local  <tempdir>/locations/primary
#>   secondary 1  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#>   secondary 2  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> History: off (store default)
#> Datasets: 1
#>   name     kind   rows     size  files  updated           1  2
#>   sales/
#>     daily  table   200  27.9 kB      2  2026-11-27 18:58  =  =
#> Secondary copies: = same, ≠ differs, – missing, ? unavailable.

env changes the prefix of the variables, so one session can use several stores: store_connect(env = "ARCHIVE") reads ARCHIVE_PRIMARY and ARCHIVE_SECONDARY. <env>_SECONDARY is read only when neither primary nor secondary is given, so a primary named in the call is never mixed with the secondaries of another store. Without a primary, the call stops and names the variable to set:

withr::with_envvar(c(STORE_PRIMARY = NA), store_connect())
#> Error in `store_connect()`:
#> ! No primary location given.
#> ℹ Pass `primary`, or set the environment variable `STORE_PRIMARY` (and `STORE_SECONDARY` for secondary locations,
#>   separated by `;`).

A secondary that cannot be reached

A primary that cannot be reached stops store_connect(): nothing can be read or written without the truth. For a secondary, it depends on what goes wrong:

  • The secondary cannot be reached (a network or credential error): store_connect() gives a warning, marks it unavailable, and reads and writes skip it.
  • The secondary answers but holds no catalogs (a local folder that does not exist, say): store_connect() stops with an error of class rcs_error_no_catalog, as for a primary. With create = TRUE it sets the location up as a new, empty store instead.
  • store_refresh() reads the catalogs of a connection again. There, a secondary that cannot be reached or holds no catalogs only gives a warning and is marked unavailable.

To show this, the folder of the second copy is moved away, as if a drive had been disconnected. store_refresh() reads the catalogs of all locations again, notices, and warns.

file.rename(copy_2, paste0(copy_2, "-away"))
#> [1] TRUE
store_refresh(st)
#> Warning: The secondary location <tempdir>/locations/copy-2 is not available; it is skipped.
#> ℹ It holds no store catalogs.
#> ℹ Run `store_refresh()` to try it again.

A write now reaches the primary and the first copy, skips the second, and says that it is behind:

store_write(st, rcs_sim_table(300, seed = 2), "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  key = c("shop_id", "date", "product"),
  partition = "year",
  mode = "replace"
)
#> ℹ Replacing "sales/daily": 300 rows in 2 files (partition year).
#> ✔ primary    <tempdir>/locations/primary  2/2 files sent  31.3 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1   2/2 files sent  31.3 kB  0.2s
#> ! secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   unavailable, skipped
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 2 files in 2 locations. Catalogs updated.
#> ! 1 secondary location is behind; run `store_sync()` to bring it up to date.

If a secondary fails during a write (a network error, say), the write goes on with the next location and reports the failed one as behind in the same way. Only a failure in the primary stops a write, and then no catalog of any location has changed.

A secondary that is behind

When the folder is back, store_refresh() finds it again. It still holds the old version of sales/daily:

file.rename(paste0(copy_2, "-away"), copy_2)
#> [1] TRUE
store_refresh(st)
st
#> ── rcs store ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Locations:
#>   primary      local  <tempdir>/locations/primary
#>   secondary 1  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#>   secondary 2  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> History: off (store default)
#> Datasets: 1
#>   name     kind   rows     size  files  updated           1  2
#>   sales/
#>     daily  table   300  31.3 kB      2  2026-11-27 18:58  =  ≠
#> Secondary copies: = same, ≠ differs, – missing, ? unavailable.

A secondary also falls behind when someone writes through a connection that does not include it:

only_primary <- store_connect(primary)
store_write(only_primary, rcs_sim_table(50, seed = 3), "sales/weekly",
  title = "Weekly sales",
  description = "Simulated weekly sales."
)
#> ℹ Writing "sales/weekly": 50 rows in 1 file.
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/locations/primary  1/1 files sent  11.7 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 1 file in 1 location. Catalogs updated.
store_refresh(st)

store_status() compares every secondary with the primary, dataset by dataset, from the catalogs alone. status is same, differs (another version), missing (not in the secondary) or extra (only in the secondary); for differs, newer says which side was written last: "source" (the primary here) or "target" (the location of the row). It is a hint only, as clocks of different machines can differ. Printed, the source is named first, and the addresses of the other locations are listed once above the table and numbered in the column location.

store_status(st)
#> Source: <tempdir>/locations/primary
#> Locations: [1] <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#>            [2] <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> # A tibble: 4 × 8
#>   dataset      location status  newer  primary_version  location_version
#>   <chr>        <chr>    <chr>   <chr>  <chr>            <chr>           
#> 1 sales/daily  [1]      same    NA     0f1993a2e5855aa8 0f1993a2e5855aa8
#> 2 sales/weekly [1]      missing NA     72f66b800c3fa743 NA              
#> 3 sales/daily  [2]      differs source 0f1993a2e5855aa8 41ec22ed5b5602ce
#> 4 sales/weekly [2]      missing NA     72f66b800c3fa743 NA              
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: primary_updated <dttm>, location_updated <dttm>

from compares every other location, the primary included, with one of the secondaries instead. The columns keep their names: primary_version and primary_updated then describe that source.

store_status(st, from = copy_2)[c("dataset", "location", "status", "newer")]
#> Source: <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> Locations: [1] <tempdir>/locations/primary
#>            [2] <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   dataset      location status  newer 
#>   <chr>        <chr>    <chr>   <chr> 
#> 1 sales/daily  [1]      differs target
#> 2 sales/weekly [1]      extra   NA    
#> 3 sales/daily  [2]      differs target

A copy that is behind is never read: reads go to a location that holds the primary’s version. The next write of a dataset brings every available secondary up to date for that dataset, whatever version it held.

Bringing secondaries up to date

store_sync() copies datasets from one location, the source, to the others, the targets: by default from the primary, every dataset that is missing or differs, to every secondary. Like a write, it copies only the files a location lacks, checks each by MD5 and switches the catalog last. By default it never deletes a dataset. dry_run = TRUE shows what it would do and changes nothing.

store_sync(st, dry_run = TRUE)
#> ℹ Dry run: nothing is changed.
#> ℹ Syncing 2 datasets from the primary <tempdir>/locations/primary to 2 secondary
#>   locations.
#> • secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1   would copy 1 dataset, 1 file (11.7 kB):
#>   "sales/weekly"
#> • secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   would copy 2 datasets, 3 files (43.0 kB):
#>   "sales/daily", "sales/weekly"

datasets and to limit it to some datasets or some secondaries. Here only the second copy is brought up to date:

store_sync(st, to = copy_2)
#> ℹ Syncing 2 datasets from the primary <tempdir>/locations/primary to 1 secondary
#>   location.
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   2 datasets, 3/3 files sent  43.0 kB  0.2s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 3 files sent to 1 location. Catalogs updated.
#> Warning: `store_sync()` replaced 1 version held by the target locations:
#> • '<tempdir>/locations/copy-2': "sales/daily" version 41ec22ed5b5602ce (updated
#>   2026-11-27 18:58:50) replaced by version 0f1993a2e5855aa8 (updated 2026-11-27 18:58:52).

store_copy() copies one dataset between any two locations of the connection, in either direction. The first copy still lacks sales/weekly; here it gets it from the second copy:

store_copy(st, "sales/weekly", from = copy_2, to = copy_1)
#> ℹ Copying "sales/weekly" (version 72f66b800c3fa743, 1 file) from
#>   <tempdir>/locations/copy-2 to
#>   <tempdir>/locations/copy-1.
#> ✔ 1/1 file sent (11.7 kB) in 0.1s, MD5 verified. Catalogs of
#>   <tempdir>/locations/copy-1 updated.
store_status(st)[c("dataset", "location", "status")]
#> Source: <tempdir>/locations/primary
#> Locations: [1] <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#>            [2] <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   dataset      location status
#>   <chr>        <chr>    <chr> 
#> 1 sales/daily  [1]      same  
#> 2 sales/weekly [1]      same  
#> 3 sales/daily  [2]      same  
#> 4 sales/weekly [2]      same

To check that a copy is sound, store_check(st, dataset) checks the dataset’s files in every available location. locations limits the check to some of them, for example store_check(st, "sales/daily", locations = copy_2).

Two more functions maintain locations. store_delete() removes a dataset from every location; it stops unless confirm repeats the full name. store_rebuild() rebuilds a location’s catalog from the small description file (manifest) that every version of every dataset leaves next to its data files, for example after a catalog file was lost.

store_delete(st, "sales/weekly", confirm = "sales/weekly")
#> ℹ Deleting "sales/weekly" and its index table from every location, keeping its history.
#> ✔ primary    <tempdir>/locations/primary  2 files deleted  11.7 kB
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1   2 files deleted  11.7 kB
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   2 files deleted  11.7 kB
#> ✔ "sales/weekly" is removed from 3 locations.
store_rebuild(st, copy_2)
#> ✔ Rebuilt the catalogs of <tempdir>/locations/copy-2: 1 dataset in 2 files, 0 earlier
#>   versions.

Syncing from a secondary

Work can also start on a secondary: on a laptop without network, say, a connection whose primary is the local copy writes there alone.

offline <- store_connect(copy_1)
store_write(offline, rcs_sim_table(80, seed = 4), "sales/monthly",
  title = "Monthly sales",
  description = "Simulated monthly sales."
)
#> ℹ Writing "sales/monthly": 80 rows in 1 file.
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1  1/1 files sent  13.1 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 1 file in 1 location. Catalogs updated.

Back on the full connection, from names the location to sync from. The targets are then every other location, the primary included; to limits them as before.

store_refresh(st)
store_sync(st, from = copy_1)
#> ℹ Syncing 2 datasets from the secondary <tempdir>/locations/copy-1 to 2 locations.
#> ✔ primary    <tempdir>/locations/primary  1 dataset, 1/1 files sent  13.1 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   1 dataset, 1/1 files sent  13.1 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 2 files sent to 2 locations. Catalogs updated.
st
#> ── rcs store ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Locations:
#>   primary      local  <tempdir>/locations/primary
#>   secondary 1  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#>   secondary 2  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> History: off (store default)
#> Datasets: 2
#>   name       kind   rows     size  files  updated           1  2
#>   sales/
#>     daily    table   300  31.3 kB      2  2026-11-27 18:58  =  =
#>     monthly  table    80  13.1 kB      1  2026-11-27 18:58  =  =
#> Secondary copies: = same, ≠ differs, – missing, ? unavailable.

Conflicts

A dataset may have changed on both sides: here sales/daily is written through a connection to the primary alone, and later through the connection to the first copy alone.

store_write(only_primary, rcs_sim_table(120, seed = 5), "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  key = c("shop_id", "date", "product"),
  partition = "year",
  mode = "replace"
)
#> ℹ Replacing "sales/daily": 120 rows in 2 files (partition year).
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/locations/primary  2/2 files sent  24.7 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 2 files in 1 location. Catalogs updated.
Sys.sleep(1)
store_write(offline, rcs_sim_table(140, seed = 6), "sales/daily",
  title = "Daily sales",
  description = "Simulated daily sales by shop and product.",
  key = c("shop_id", "date", "product"),
  partition = "year",
  mode = "replace"
)
#> ℹ Replacing "sales/daily": 140 rows in 2 files (partition year).
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1  2/2 files sent  25.8 kB  0.1s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 2 files in 1 location. Catalogs updated.
store_refresh(st)

A sync from the primary finds that the first copy holds another version that was written later than the primary’s: a conflict. That dataset is not copied there. Everything else goes ahead (here the second copy, which held an older version, gets the primary’s, and a warning lists the version it replaced); after the last target the call stops with an error of class rcs_error_sync_conflict that lists every conflict. The condition’s field result holds the result table, so a script can inspect it.

store_sync(st)
#> ℹ Syncing 2 datasets from the primary <tempdir>/locations/primary to 2 secondary
#>   locations.
#> ✖ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1   1 conflict, newer here: "sales/daily"
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   1 dataset, 2/2 files sent  24.7 kB  0.2s
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 2 files sent to 1 location. Catalogs updated.
#> Warning: `store_sync()` replaced 1 version held by the target locations:
#> • '<tempdir>/locations/copy-2': "sales/daily" version 0f1993a2e5855aa8 (updated
#>   2026-11-27 18:58:52) replaced by version 98d066b5654644d4 (updated 2026-11-27 18:58:57).
#> Error in `store_sync()`:
#> ! 1 dataset was not copied: the target holds a newer version.
#> ✖ '<tempdir>/locations/copy-1': "sales/daily" version 7f31826d9513c336 (updated
#>   2026-11-27 18:58:58) is newer than the source's version 98d066b5654644d4 (updated 2026-11-27 18:58:57).
#> ℹ The other copies and deletions were made.
#> ℹ Run with `force = TRUE` to copy the source over it, or sync from the location that holds the newer version.

Conflicts are detected by the times of the last writes recorded in the catalogs, which come from the clocks of the machines that wrote. Decide which version to keep: to keep the primary’s, force = TRUE copies it over the newer one, and the warning names the version that was replaced. To keep the copy’s, sync from the copy instead.

store_sync(st, force = TRUE)
#> ℹ Syncing 2 datasets from the primary <tempdir>/locations/primary to 2 secondary
#>   locations.
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1   1 dataset, 2/2 files sent  24.7 kB  0.2s
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   up to date
#> ✔ MD5 identical for 2 files sent to 1 location. Catalogs updated.
#> Warning: `store_sync()` replaced 1 version held by the target locations:
#> • '<tempdir>/locations/copy-1': "sales/daily" version 7f31826d9513c336 (updated
#>   2026-11-27 18:58:58) replaced by version 98d066b5654644d4 (updated 2026-11-27 18:58:57).

When the source is the newer side, the copy goes ahead without force; the warning (class rcs_warning_sync_overwrite) still lists every target version that was overwritten.

Deletions

A dataset deleted in one location stays in the others: store_status() shows it there as extra, and a sync leaves it alone. delete = TRUE deletes from each target the datasets the source no longer holds, with their index tables, after the copies; history versions are kept, as with store_delete(history = FALSE). datasets limits the deletions too.

Here sales/monthly is deleted on the first copy only, then the deletion is synced from there:

store_delete(offline, "sales/monthly", confirm = "sales/monthly")
#> ℹ Deleting "sales/monthly" and its index table from every location, keeping its history.
#> ✔ primary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1  2 files deleted  13.1 kB
#> ✔ "sales/monthly" is removed from 1 location.
store_refresh(st)
store_sync(st, from = copy_1, delete = TRUE)
#> ℹ Syncing 1 dataset from the secondary <tempdir>/locations/copy-1 to 2 locations.
#> ! primary    <tempdir>/locations/primary  1 dataset kept, delete on primary needs
#>   force: "sales/monthly"
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   1 dataset deleted: "sales/monthly"
#> ✔ 1 dataset deleted in 1 location.
#> ! 1 dataset kept in the primary: delete on primary needs force (`force = TRUE`).

The second copy lost the dataset, but the primary kept it: deleting from the primary, the truth of the store, also needs force = TRUE. Until then the result lists it in the column kept.

store_sync(st, from = copy_1, delete = TRUE, force = TRUE)
#> ℹ Syncing 1 dataset from the secondary <tempdir>/locations/copy-1 to 2 locations.
#> ✔ primary    <tempdir>/locations/primary  1 dataset deleted: "sales/monthly"
#> ✔ secondary  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2   up to date
#> ✔ 1 dataset deleted in 1 location.
st
#> ── rcs store ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Locations:
#>   primary      local  <tempdir>/locations/primary
#>   secondary 1  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#>   secondary 2  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-2
#> History: off (store default)
#> Datasets: 1
#>   name     kind   rows     size  files  updated           1  2
#>   sales/
#>     daily  table   120  24.7 kB      2  2026-11-27 18:58  =  =
#> Secondary copies: = same, ≠ differs, – missing, ? unavailable.

Deletions run also when conflicts were found, and are reported with them.

Cloud locations

A Google Cloud Storage location is given by its address. Nothing else changes: the same functions work on buckets and on folders, in any mix.

# A bucket alone
st <- store_connect("gs://my-bucket/store")

# A bucket as primary, a local copy for fast reads
st <- store_connect("gs://my-bucket/store", secondary = "~/data/my-store")

# Two buckets and a local copy
st <- store_connect("gs://my-bucket/store",
  secondary = c("~/data/my-store", "gs://other-bucket/store")
)

# A new, empty store in a bucket
store_create("gs://my-bucket/new-store")

Data are streamed: a read with filters fetches only the files and blocks of rows it needs, without downloading whole datasets.

Credentials

Four clients of the package talk to Google Cloud Storage: Arrow reads data and copies files (the installed arrow package must support GCS: arrow::arrow_with_gcs() returns TRUE); the storage JSON API reads the MD5 checksums of stored files, so that files need not be downloaded to be verified (it needs the packages gargle and httr2); GDAL reads rasters through its /vsigs/ path; and DuckDB reads data files when a store is opened in DuckDB (see vignette("duckdb")). They all get their credentials from the connection: set them once, with the argument auth of store_connect() or store_create(), and every client uses them. No environment variable is needed or changed.

Without auth, every bucket location uses rcs_auth_gcs(), the default lookup. It is a chain in which the first variable that is set decides; it does not fall through to the next step:

  1. when the environment variable GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS is set, the key file it names, and only that file: a missing file is an error (class rcs_error_backend);
  2. else, when CLOUDSDK_CONFIG is set, application_default_credentials.json in that folder only; gcloud’s own folder is not tried;
  3. else the same file in gcloud’s own folder (%APPDATA%/gcloud on Windows, ~/.config/gcloud elsewhere), written once by gcloud auth application-default login;
  4. when the file of step 2 or 3 does not exist, ambient credentials: Arrow and the JSON API use Google’s own defaults, such as the machine’s account on Google Cloud. GDAL and DuckDB cannot use these.

For a personal account, the usual setup is therefore one command in a terminal, once per machine, and nothing in R:

gcloud auth application-default login

rcs_auth_gcs() also takes a credential explicitly: key is a JSON key file, of a service account or of a user login; token is an access token obtained elsewhere; fun is a function that returns a fresh token each time it is called. auth accepts such an object, the path of a key file, or a list named by address that gives each location its own credential (locations left out use the default lookup):

# A service account for every bucket of the connection
st <- store_connect("gs://my-bucket/store",
  auth = rcs_auth_gcs(key = "~/keys/reader.json")
)

# The same, with the path alone
st <- store_connect("gs://my-bucket/store", auth = "~/keys/reader.json")

# One credential per location
st <- store_connect("gs://my-bucket/store",
  secondary = c("~/data/my-store", "gs://other-bucket/store"),
  auth = list(
    "gs://my-bucket/store" = "~/keys/reader.json",
    "gs://other-bucket/store" = rcs_auth_gcs(fun = my_token_function)
  )
)

Tokens of a key file or a function are renewed five minutes before they expire, so a long session never needs to sign in again; a token given directly cannot be renewed and lasts as long as its issuer allows, usually an hour. Asking for the same source twice gives the same object, with its token. Printing a credential never contacts the network and never shows a secret; the identity (the account’s e-mail) is known after the first token:

rcs_auth_gcs(token = "<an access token>")
#> <rcs_auth_gcs>
#> Source:   an access token given to rcs_auth_gcs(token = )
#> Identity: known after the first token
#> Token:    given by the caller, not renewed

Credentials are never written to files, catalogs or logs, nor put in environment variables, with one exception: GDAL’s options are process-wide. Reading a raster from a bucket gives GDAL the credential of that location (the three GS_OAUTH2_* options for a user login, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS as a GDAL option for a service account, an Authorization header for a token or a function), and it applies to every GDAL read in the R process. Reading rasters through two connections with different credentials therefore switches GDAL from one to the other; the first switch warns (class rcs_warning_gdal_credential), because a raster opened with the previous credential reads its tiles lazily and may fail on its next read. Also, GDAL remembers a failed open: after a credential problem is fixed, a raster that failed may need a new R session.

DuckDB gets a temporary secret in its own connection, made from the location’s token. A secret holds a token, not a key: after about an hour of DuckDB work on a bucket, call store_duckdb() again to refresh it.

store_auth_check() tries each client on each location with a small probe and reports, without stopping, which work. Local folders need no credentials; each local location gives one row (the column location, the address, is left out here):

store_auth_check(st)[c("client", "ok", "note")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   client ok    note                               
#>   <chr>  <lgl> <chr>                              
#> 1 all    TRUE  local folder: no credentials needed
#> 2 all    TRUE  local folder: no credentials needed
#> 3 all    TRUE  local folder: no credentials needed

On a bucket it gives one row per client: Arrow and the JSON API look up the catalog file, GDAL opens the first raster of the location (ok is NA when there is none), and DuckDB counts the rows of the catalog (NA when duckdb is not installed):

st <- store_connect("gs://my-bucket/store")
store_auth_check(st)

When a location cannot be reached, the error names the credential in use and how to pass another one with auth. A primary that cannot be reached stops store_connect(); a secondary that cannot be reached gives a warning and is skipped (see “A secondary that cannot be reached”).

History per connection

Whether replaced versions are kept is a setting of the store (store_create(history = )), which a connection can override for its own writes, and a dataset for itself (see vignette("rcs")). This store keeps no history by default; a connection can keep it for its own writes:

st_keep <- store_connect(primary, secondary = copy_1, history = TRUE)
st_keep
#> ── rcs store ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Locations:
#>   primary      local  <tempdir>/locations/primary
#>   secondary 1  local  <tempdir>/locations/copy-1
#> History: on (this connection; store default off)
#> Datasets: 1
#>   name     kind   rows     size  files  updated           1
#>   sales/
#>     daily  table   120  24.7 kB      2  2026-11-27 18:58  =
#> Secondary copies: = same, ≠ differs, – missing, ? unavailable.
